title: Sensex, Nifty Fall for Fourth Session as Brent Crude Hits $114
excerpt: Benchmarks lost 2.2% and 2.4% this week as crude surged on Saudi supply fears and foreign investors sold Rs 3,458.70 crore in a single session, while small-caps posted their worst week in 20 months.
body:
• Sensex closed at 73,123.83, down 125.56 points or 0.17%, and the Nifty 50 settled at 22,600, down 87.65 points or 0.39% on Friday, October 23 — a fourth straight losing session that left the indexes down 2.2% and 2.4% for the week.
  • Brent crude surged to about $114 a barrel on supply fears after attacks on top exporter Saudi Arabia by Yemen's Houthis, according to The Hindu BusinessLine.
  • Foreign institutional investors net sold Rs 3,458.70 crore of Indian equities in the previous session, while domestic institutional investors net bought Rs 2,891.32 crore; foreign portfolio investors have pulled Rs 48,211 crore out of Indian equities in October through October 22, according to NSDL data.
  • Broader stocks were hit hardest — small-caps lost 7.3% and mid-caps 5.6% this week, their worst week in 20 months — but strategists say more than Rs 3 lakh crore of Jio Platforms IPO money returning after allotment by Monday could support large-caps next week.

Indian equity benchmarks reversed early gains to close lower for a fourth consecutive session on Friday, as a surge in crude oil prices to about $114 a barrel and continued foreign investor selling outweighed domestic institutional buying. The Sensex fell more than 1,000 points from its intraday high before recovering part of the loss, and the Nifty slipped below 22,500 during the session before closing at 22,600.

Crude at $114 drives the sell-off

Sentiment turned after Brent crude futures rose to about $114 on energy supply fears following attacks on Saudi Arabia, the world's top oil exporter, by Yemen's Houthis, The Hindu BusinessLine reported. For India, which imports most of its crude, sustained prices at this level raise the import bill, pressure the rupee and add to inflation risks through higher transport and manufacturing costs. The rupee closed at 94.94 against the US dollar on Friday, little changed for the week after oil-driven declines erased early gains.

"Brent crude spiking to $114 is a major negative for the economy and markets."

— V K Vijayakumar, Chief Investment Strategist, Geojit Investments Limited

Vijayakumar added that there are counterweights: the US 10-year yield has declined to 4.96% and the rupee had appreciated to 94.70 to the dollar earlier, both of which can restrain foreign selling. Fifteen of the 16 major sectors logged weekly losses, with metal, realty and banking shares among the steepest decliners on Friday, while information technology stocks showed relative resilience, with TCS, Infosys and HCL Technologies attracting buying, according to DSIJ's closing report.

Foreign selling, domestic cushion

Foreign institutional investors were net sellers of Rs 3,458.70 crore in the previous session, extending a heavy October withdrawal — NSDL data show foreign portfolio investors have pulled Rs 48,211 crore from Indian equities this month through October 22, taking 2026 net outflows to about Rs 3.10 lakh crore. Domestic institutional investors bought Rs 2,891.32 crore in the same session, their third straight session of net buying, which cushioned the benchmarks but not the broader market. Market breadth was sharply negative: 3,011 stocks declined against 624 advances on the NSE, and 655 stocks touched 52-week lows against 23 at 52-week highs.

What to watch next week

The week's trade was also drained by demand for the Jio Platforms IPO, which drew bids of 13.8 times by Friday's close. Vijayakumar noted that more than Rs 3 lakh crore of the roughly Rs 3.73 lakh crore that went into the Jio Platforms IPO over the past two days will return to the system after allotment is completed by next Monday, a potential liquidity surge that could lift the market next week, with any rally likely led by fairly valued large-caps. The risk remains crude: as long as Brent holds near $114, oil-sensitive sectors including automobiles, paints, aviation and oil marketing companies stay exposed to rising input costs, and foreign flows are likely to remain volatile.
